attacks.name: AI Fabricated Identity
attacks.what_attacker_needs: A generative model, a handful of real customer profiles to imitate, and a way to submit new accounts (open API or web form).
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: Each individual transaction looks statistically normal because the AI copies real spending shape. There is no prior history to compare against, so rules based on velocity don't fire on transaction #1.
attacks.damage: New account fraud, promo abuse, mule accounts used to launder stolen funds.
attacks.simulated_by: agent1_fake_identity, real OpenAI GPT-4o-mini calls generating each identity

attacks.name: Spending Pattern Replication (Card Testing & Draining)
attacks.what_attacker_needs: A stolen card number or token, and a generator that mimics the cardholder's usual amount/merchant/timing shape while executing at machine speed.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: Amounts and merchants resemble genuine history; the anomaly is velocity and cumulative volume, which only shows up in aggregate, not per transaction.
attacks.damage: Direct monetary loss, chargebacks, card network penalties.

attacks.name: Payment Form / API Fuzzing
attacks.stage: Client side input into backend processing
attacks.what_attacker_needs: Knowledge of the form/API schema and an automated fuzzer that throws malformed, oversized, or injection style payloads at each field.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: Individually loud and easy to flag, but attackers use it as reconnaissance: the one field that doesn't reject cleanly becomes the entry point for a quieter attack later.
attacks.damage: Backend crashes, injection vulnerabilities, data exposure, or a discovered bypass used in a later attack.
attacks.simulated_by: agent6_injection_generator, known public payloads, no LLM needed

attacks.name: AI Voice/Chat Social Engineering
attacks.what_attacker_needs: A voice cloning or conversational model, some public/leaked personal data about the victim, and a target support channel.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: Convincingly mimics a real customer's voice or writing style well enough to pass authentication questions based on personal knowledge.
attacks.damage: Account takeover, unauthorized card issuance, disabled fraud alerts.
attacks.simulated_by: agent2_social_engineer, real OpenAI calls generating text call transcripts only. No voice cloning, no audio, no real support line contacted

attacks.name: Authorization Limit Probing
attacks.what_attacker_needs: A stolen card and a script that submits many small transactions across merchants to map out fraud detection thresholds before making one large charge.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: Each probe is small enough to sit under thresholds set per transaction; the pattern only becomes visible when probes are correlated across merchants.
attacks.damage: Reveals the exact threshold defenders use, which is then exploited in a larger, precisely sized fraudulent charge.
attacks.simulated_by: agent3_limit_prober, real: submits amounts $10 to $10,000 through our own trained detector and reads back its real decision boundary

attacks.name: AI Generated KYC Document Forgery
attacks.what_attacker_needs: An image generation model capable of producing plausible ID documents or selfies that pass automated liveness/document checks.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: Generated documents can be tuned specifically to defeat the exact verification model in use if the attacker has query access to it.
attacks.damage: Bypasses KYC entirely, enabling fully synthetic identities to open accounts that pass verification.
attacks.simulated_by: agent4_kyc_forger, real OpenAI calls generating identity metadata bundles only, no document images, then scored by our own detector

attacks.name: Feedback Loop Poisoning of the Fraud Model
attacks.what_attacker_needs: Repeated small transactions plus false dispute/chargeback signals designed to teach the detector's retraining pipeline to treat fraud patterns as normal.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: Attacks the training data, not the transaction. By the time it's visible, the model itself has drifted toward tolerating the fraud pattern.
attacks.damage: Long term degradation of detection accuracy; hardest to detect because the model's own confidence goes up, not down.
attacks.simulated_by: not simulated in this lab (known gap). agent7_feedback_loop is related but distinct: it generates real time evasion variants against the trained model, it does not poison a retraining pipeline

attacks.name: AI Orchestrated Business Email Compromise / Vendor Payment Redirection
attacks.stage: Accounts payable and vendor invoicing (B2B wire/ACH rails)
attacks.what_attacker_needs: A compromised or spoofed vendor email account plus an LLM that drafts a convincing updated bank details request matching the real vendor's tone and invoicing history.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: Wire and ACH payments have no real time chargeback, so the redirection is only noticed after the funds are gone. GenAI mimics a specific vendor's writing style from leaked or scraped correspondence rather than a generic phishing template.
attacks.damage: Direct, often unrecoverable, large dollar loss on B2B payment rails.
attacks.simulated_by: not simulated in this lab (known gap). Out of scope for agents targeting consumer/card rails; would need vendor correspondence data this lab doesn't generate

attacks.name: Authorized Push Payment Fraud via Voice Cloned Urgency Scams
attacks.what_attacker_needs: A cloned or synthesized voice of a trusted contact (bank fraud department, family member) plus manufactured urgency to bypass the customer's own scrutiny.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: The customer authorizes the transfer themselves; no stolen credential, no anomalous authentication. Velocity and pattern similarity features don't fire because the transaction looks entirely intentional.
attacks.damage: Instant, often irreversible transfer; push payment rails settle faster than dispute processes can intervene.
attacks.simulated_by: not simulated in this lab (known gap). A shape based classifier scores transaction shape, not authorization intent, so this sits outside what it can see by construction

attacks.name: Agentic Commerce Hijack: Prompt Injection Against Autonomous Shopping Agents
attacks.stage: AI shopping/checkout agents transacting on a customer's behalf
attacks.what_attacker_needs: A malicious merchant page or third party content embedding hidden instructions an LLM driven purchasing agent reads and acts on.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: The transaction is initiated by an agent the customer trusts, using real, authorized payment credentials. The compromise happens upstream, in what the agent was instructed to do, not in the payment itself.
attacks.damage: Unauthorized purchases, shipping address redirection, or budget exhaustion via what looks like a normal agent initiated transaction.
attacks.simulated_by: not simulated in this lab (known gap). The mandate layer's merchant whitelist, spending limit, and time restriction would still catch some of these in practice, a real if partial mitigation

attacks.name: Deepfake Liveness Bypass for Biometric KYC
attacks.what_attacker_needs: Real time face swap or diffusion based video generation that can respond to a liveness challenge (blink, turn head) convincingly.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: Modern liveness checks exist specifically to defend against this; a high fidelity real time deepfake defeats the exact signal the check relies on.
attacks.damage: Full KYC bypass for synthetic or stolen identities, more severe than static document forgery since it defeats the strongest KYC defense in use.
attacks.simulated_by: not simulated in this lab (known gap). agent4_kyc_forger generates identity metadata only, no video, so this stays a distinct gap

attacks.name: AI Generated Fake Dispute Evidence (Chargeback / Refund Abuse)
attacks.stage: Post transaction dispute and chargeback process
attacks.what_attacker_needs: An LLM or image model that fabricates convincing but fake evidence (a doctored receipt, a generated item photo, a fabricated support transcript) to win a dispute on a legitimate transaction.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: The underlying transaction was genuine; the fraud happens entirely in paperwork submitted afterward, a stage most fraud detection never inspects.
attacks.damage: Direct merchant loss via friendly fraud at a scale automation makes newly cheap, plus network chargeback penalties.
attacks.simulated_by: not simulated in this lab (known gap). Related to but distinct from model_poisoning: this targets the dispute adjudication process, not the fraud model's training signal

attacks.name: Synthetic Identity Bust Out
attacks.stage: Full account lifecycle, monetized in a single terminal event
attacks.what_attacker_needs: A fabricated identity used to build months of genuinely unremarkable transaction history and a real credit line, then maxed out and abandoned in one final burst.
attacks.why_hard_to_catch: Every step before the bust out looks identical to genuine account seasoning. There is no anomaly to detect until the single terminal transaction, after months of history have already vouched for the account.
attacks.damage: Full credit line loss, concentrated in a single terminal event after a long dormant period disproportionate to how the account looked day to day.
attacks.simulated_by: not simulated in this lab (known gap). A per transaction classifier scoring each transaction independently cannot see a pattern spanning months, a real limitation of that design
